text.tspan: Police have **retained** duties involving *crime, threat, harm, violence, safeguarding, terrorism, serious organised crime, and emergency response*.
Police have **lost** duties involving *nuisance, environmental enforcement, parking, noise, local disorder, and civil regulation*,
which have been transferred to councils or civil enforcement bodies.
Parking, environmental offences, and nuisance behaviours were reclassified as **civil matters**, enabling councils to issue fines and hire enforcement officers.
This followed the **Traffic Management Act 2004**, later expanded through local authority powers.
The 2026 Home Office white paper emphasises removing “barriers that stop the police focusing on the public’s priorities” — meaning **serious crime, violence,
HMICFRS annual assessments show police forces under “increasing strain as crime, threats and expectations change,” leading to withdrawal from low‑level duties.
This created a **parallel civic‑order enforcement system**.
highlight **loitering** — and specifically **“loitering” and “loitering with intent”** — as a *major* lost policing duty and
a structural contributor to civic‑decay dynamics.
It wasn’t omitted because it’s minor; it’s one of the **most symbolically important losses**,
because it represents the withdrawal of police from **street‑level guardianship**,
the very visible “thin blue line” that once deterred opportunistic crime, intimidation, and antisocial congregation.
now this explicitly include: LOITERING & LOITERING WITH INTENT FULLY INTEGRATED
- **Loitering with intent** (historically tied to stop‑and‑account, suspicious circumstances, and pre‑emptive intervention)
- Their **linkages** to your broader civic‑decay schema (street‑corner disorder, ASB clusters, withdrawal of guardianship, fragmentation of responsibility)
# **Why Loitering Is a Critical Civic‑Decay Node**
### **1. It was once a cornerstone of “street guardianship”**
From the 1960s through the early 2000s, police routinely:
Wardens have **no powers** equivalent to police.
- street corners become informal power zones
This is textbook **Broken Windows Theory**, but with the twist that the *state has withdrawn*.
This is the **fragmentation of responsibility** mapping.==
PART 1 — A Follow‑On Table Focused Solely on Loitering & Loitering With Intent**
*(Integrated into the policing‑duties framework, but treated as its own dedicated table because of its civic‑decay significance.)*
### **G. Loitering & Loitering With Intent — Duty Evolution Table (1960 → 2026)**
| Duty Area | 1960–1980 | 1980–2000 | 2000–2010 | 2010–2026 | Current Responsible Body | Civic‑Decay Impact |

| **Loitering (general)** | Police routinely dispersed groups; visible street guardianship | Still enforced; used to prevent intimidation & disorder | Gradual reduction; prioritisation shifts | Police withdrawal; councils/wardens have no equivalent powers | Councils (ASB teams), PCSOs (limited) | Loss of deterrence; street‑corner disorder; informal power zones |

| **Loitering with intent** (suspicious circumstances) | Police used stop‑and‑account; early intervention | Strong preventative tool; pre‑emptive crime disruption | Increasing constraints; evidential thresholds rise | Largely abandoned except where crime suspected | No replacement body; councils cannot intervene | Vacuum in early‑stage crime prevention; intimidation rises |

| **Street‑corner dispersal** | Police enforced movement; prevented territorial behaviour | Still common; used to break up groups | Reduced due to resource pressure | Councils rely on PSPOs; police rarely attend | Councils (PSPO enforcement) | Territoriality increases; residents withdraw from public space |

| **Suspicious behaviour challenge** | Police challenged individuals; deterrent effect | Still routine | Declines sharply | Only used when threat/harm identified | Police (rarely), councils (never) | Loss of preventative policing; escalation of ASB |
| **Preventative patrol presence** | High visibility; cornerstone of order | Still present | Reduced | Targeted only; not routine | PCSOs | Weakens social norms; increases signal disorder |
| **Pre‑emptive intervention** | Police intervened before crime occurred | Still common | Declines | Almost gone | No replacement | Systemic erosion; fragmentation of responsibility |
This is a **four‑era narrative**, each panel showing the policing model, the powers, the cultural norms, and the civic‑decay consequences.
- “Move along, please” was a standard tool
- Residents felt ownership of public space
- Police acted as **guardians of social norms**
## **Panel 2 — 1980s: The Era of Assertive Public‑Order Policing**
- Residents retained confidence in public space
---## **Panel 3 — 2000s: The Era of Resource Pressure & Policy Shift**
- Rising demand (domestic abuse, safeguarding, serious crime)
- Residents began withdrawing from public space
## **Panel 4 — 2010–2026: The Era of Harm‑Based Policing & Full Withdrawal**
- Police intervene only when threat/violence present
- Loitering no longer a police matter
- Councils/wardens handle ASB but cannot intervene on suspicion
- Antisocial noise becomes a dominance signal
- The state has withdrawn from early‑stage disorder
- Citizens no longer know who is responsible
## **1. Loitering was a cornerstone of street guardianship**
Removing this function removes the **first line of defence** against disorder.
This creates a **power vacuum** in public space.
Loitering is a **signal disorder** — a visible marker that:
This is **Broken Windows Theory**, but with a twist:
The state has **abandoned the window entirely**.
This is the **fragmentation of responsibility**, a hallmark of systemic erosion.
